title: Consumers Report Significant Improvements in Credit Market Experiences and Expectations

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York released results from its June 2015 SCE Credit Access Survey, showing significant improvements in consumer credit market experiences and expectations. The share of successful credit applicants reached a new high since the survey began in October 2013, while rejection rates and discouraged credit seekers both reached new series lows.
key_points: 40.9 percent of respondents applied for credit over the last 12 months and were granted credit, reaching a new series high
Rejection rates per applicant decreased from 20.0 percent to 13.8 percent, reaching a new series low
For credit scores under 680, the proportion of accepted applicants increased by 11.8 percentage points and rejected applicants decreased by 10.3 percentage points
Rejection rates for the lowest creditworthy group dropped to 33.4 percent from 52.6 percent in February 2015
6.6 percent of respondents were too discouraged to apply despite indicating a need for credit, reaching a new series low
Average likelihood of applying for mortgage, auto loan, and credit card limit increase applications reached new series highs
why_it_matters: The survey provides detailed insight into the credit market structure by tracking consumer experiences and expectations across different credit products, demographics, and credit score groups. The substantial decline in rejection rates, particularly for lower creditworthy consumers, suggests meaningful easing in credit access conditions.
market_structure_context: The SCE Credit Access Survey provides structured data on credit market structure, tracking application rates, approval rates, rejection rates, and discouraged borrowers across credit products (auto loans, credit cards, credit card limit increases, mortgages, mortgage refinancing). The survey breaks down results by age group and credit score subgroup.
important_numbers: 29% likely to apply for at least one credit type over next 12 months

human_review.notes: Historical research paper from 2015 NY Fed Credit Access Survey. Relevant to credit market structure but dated and unlikely to have direct market impact in current context. Human review recommended to assess archival value.
